# 2 Samuel Chapter 24 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 197r–198v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_024_page_001.jpg, 2SA_024_page_002.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah."

**2** So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, that I may know the number of the people."

**3** But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it. But why does my lord the king desire this thing?"

**4** But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to count the people of Israel.

**5** They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, to the south of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and toward Jazer.

**6** Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and they came to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon.

**7** They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites, and they went out to the south of Judah at Beersheba.

**8** When they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.

**9** And Joab gave the number of the census of the people to the king: in Israel there were eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand.

**10** But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."

**11** When David rose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to Gad the prophet, David's seer, saying,

**12** "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD: Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

**13** So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall seven years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your enemies while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days of pestilence in your land? Now consider and decide what answer I shall return to the one who sent me."

**14** Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercies are great; but let me not fall into the hand of man."

**15** So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning until the appointed time, and there died of the people from Dan to Beersheba seventy thousand men.

**16** And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented concerning the disaster, and said to the angel who was working destruction among the people, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

**17** Then David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wrong. But these, the sheep — what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."

**18** And Gad came to David that day and said to him, "Go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."

**19** So David went up, according to the word of Gad, as the LORD commanded.

**20** And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming toward him. And Araunah went out and bowed down before the king with his face to the ground.

**21** And Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be averted from the people."

**22** Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood."

**23** All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you."

**24** But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

**25** And David built there an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD was entreated for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the narrative arc: the incitement to census (v.1), the census itself (vv.2-9), David's repentance (v.10), the three choices (vv.11-13), David's choice and its consequences (vv.14-15), the angel's halt at Jerusalem (v.16), David's intercession (v.17), and the purchase of the threshing floor and the building of the altar (vv.18-25). The key theological issues — the identity of the inciter (YHWH vs. Satan), the seven-vs-three years variant, David's "heart struck him," and the cost of genuine worship — are noted by all three. This chapter closes the book of 2 Samuel with sacrifice and divine mercy, and all translators recognize its forward-pointing significance to the Temple.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "incited" vs. "stirred up"
- **EMET:** "he-incited [vayyaset] David"
- **LOGOS:** "he incited David"
- **PNEUMA:** "He stirred up David"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "he incited David." EMET/LOGOS's "incited" is the more precise rendering of *vayyaset*, which implies provocation. PNEUMA's "stirred up" softens the theological difficulty.

### V.3 — "why does my lord the king desire this?" vs. "why on earth does my lord the king want to do this?"
- **EMET:** "why does-my-lord the-king desire [chafets] this thing?"
- **LOGOS:** "But why does my lord the king desire this thing?"
- **PNEUMA:** "But why on earth does my lord the king want to do this?"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "But why does my lord the king desire this thing?" LOGOS's formality is appropriate for Joab's formal address to the king. PNEUMA's "why on earth" is colloquial.

### V.10 — "David's heart struck him" vs. "David was stricken with guilt"
- **EMET:** "struck [the]-heart of-David him"
- **LOGOS:** "David's heart struck him"
- **PNEUMA:** "David was stricken with guilt"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "David's heart struck him." EMET/LOGOS preserve the remarkable Hebrew idiom. PNEUMA's "stricken with guilt" is accurate in meaning but loses the vivid image of conscience as a physical blow.

### V.10 — "I have been very foolish" vs. "I have been an utter fool"
- **EMET:** "I-have-been-very-foolish [niskalti me'od]"
- **LOGOS:** "I have acted very foolishly"
- **PNEUMA:** "I have been an utter fool"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "I have acted very foolishly." LOGOS best captures the verbal form *niskalti* while maintaining register.

### V.13 — "know and see" vs. "consider and decide" vs. "think it over"
- **EMET:** "Now know and-see"
- **LOGOS:** "Now consider and decide"
- **PNEUMA:** "Think it over and tell me"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Now consider and decide." LOGOS balances the two Hebrew imperatives with natural English.

### V.14 — "I am in great distress" vs. "This is agonizing"
- **EMET:** "I-am-in-great-distress [tsar-li me'od]"
- **LOGOS:** "I am in great distress"
- **PNEUMA:** "This is agonizing"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "I am in great distress." EMET/LOGOS are closer to the Hebrew *tsar-li*. PNEUMA's "agonizing" is vivid but shifts the idiom.

### V.16 — "relented" vs. "was grieved"
- **EMET:** "relented [vayyinnachem]"
- **LOGOS:** "relented"
- **PNEUMA:** "was grieved"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "relented." EMET/LOGOS follow the standard translation of *vayyinnachem* in this context. PNEUMA's "was grieved" captures one aspect of the root but does not convey the change in action.

### V.16 — "Enough; now withdraw your hand" vs. "Enough! Pull back your hand" vs. "stay your hand"
- **EMET:** "Enough [rav]! Now withdraw [heref] your-hand"
- **LOGOS:** "It is enough; now stay your hand"
- **PNEUMA:** "Enough! Pull back your hand"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "It is enough; now stay your hand." LOGOS's rendering is the most dignified and natural. "Stay your hand" is an English idiom that perfectly matches the Hebrew *heref yadekha*.

### V.17 — "the flock" vs. "these, the sheep" vs. "they are just sheep"
- **EMET:** "these, the-flock [ha-tson]"
- **LOGOS:** "these, the sheep"
- **PNEUMA:** "they are just sheep"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "these, the sheep." LOGOS preserves the Hebrew's demonstrative structure. PNEUMA's "just sheep" adds a diminutive sense ("merely") that intensifies beyond the Hebrew.

### V.24 — "buying I will buy" vs. "I will buy" vs. "I insist on paying"
- **EMET:** "buying I-will-buy [qanoh eqneh]"
- **LOGOS:** "I will buy it from you for a price"
- **PNEUMA:** "I insist on paying you a fair price"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "I will buy it from you for a price." LOGOS renders the emphasis of the infinitive absolute through the prepositional phrase "for a price." PNEUMA's "I insist" captures the emphasis differently but adds words.

### V.25 — "was entreated" vs. "answered the prayers"
- **EMET:** "was-entreated [vaye'ater] YHWH for-the-land"
- **LOGOS:** "the LORD was entreated for the land"
- **PNEUMA:** "The LORD answered the prayers for the land"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the LORD was entreated for the land." EMET/LOGOS preserve the Hebrew passive construction *vaye'ater*. PNEUMA's "answered the prayers" is interpretive.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
